title: Smelter Stack Beside the Estate
scenario: Plant manager Oluwaseun Bakare in Port Harcourt, Nigeria, runs a metal recycling facility that employs 700 people, most from the nearby informal settlement. Residents report coughing and blackened washing, and a university study links the plant to elevated lead in children's blood. Installing filters costs roughly a year's profit and would require a two-month shutdown. Competing facilities abroad have lower standards. He must decide before the regulator's annual audit.
options: Shut down for two months to install the filters, protecting children's health and accepting lost wages and profit.
Install the filters in phases without a shutdown, reducing emissions more slowly while keeping wages flowing.
Contest the study's findings and delay investment until independent testing confirms the source of the lead.

title: Incinerator Beside the Primary School
scenario: City engineer Magdalena Rojas in Santiago, Chile, must choose a site for a waste-to-energy incinerator. The cheapest, best-connected site lies beside a low-income neighbourhood and a primary school, where air quality is already poor. A wealthier district offers a site that costs 30 percent more and would raise fees citywide. The existing landfill is nearly full, and a decision is required this quarter.
options: Choose the cheaper site by the low-income neighbourhood, keeping costs low for all residents and proceeding quickly.
Choose the costlier site in the wealthier district, accepting higher fees to avoid adding to an already burdened community.
Choose the cheaper site but fund strict emissions controls, health monitoring and community benefits for the neighbourhood.
tension: distributive justice vs. cost to the public

title: The Pipeline Easement on Reserve Land
scenario: Tribal council attorney Marcus Eagleheart in Alberta, Canada, advises a First Nation that has been offered a large payment for an easement across its land for an oil pipeline. The route avoids the main settlement but crosses the river that supplies it. The payment would fund housing and a treatment plant that the community lacks. Elders worry about spills, while younger members want jobs. The council must give its answer at the end of the week.
options: Advise accepting the easement with strong spill insurance and monitoring, using the payment to meet urgent housing and water needs.
Advise declining the easement, protecting the river and the community's long-term sovereignty over its land.
Advise negotiating for equity ownership and a rerouting study, a path that could take years and lose the offer.

title: Tannery Wastewater and the Tanners' Union
scenario: Environmental inspector Nasreen Chowdhury in Dhaka has found that a cluster of leather tanneries is discharging untreated chromium waste into a canal used by downstream families for washing and fishing. Closing the tanneries would put around 5,000 workers out of work, and the factories claim they cannot afford treatment systems. A government treatment plant has been delayed for years. She has the authority to issue a closure order or a conditional warning.
options: Issue closure orders to the worst offenders, protecting the downstream community's health despite job losses.
Issue a conditional warning with a firm deadline, giving the factories a chance to comply while the pollution continues.
Close all tanneries until the shared treatment plant is built, imposing broad hardship to force government action.

title: Cheaper Homes on the Old Gasworks
scenario: Developer and former social worker Priya Raghunathan in Manchester, England, has the chance to build 200 affordable homes on a former gasworks site. Remediation to the legal standard is complete, but independent soil tests show some residual contaminants that regulators consider acceptable. Additional cleaning would raise costs and force a cut of forty homes. The council housing list is long and residents would be low-income families. She needs to confirm her plans this month.
options: Build as planned to the legal standard, delivering all two hundred homes to families who urgently need them.
Fund additional cleaning and build only 160 homes, reducing health risks at the cost of fewer families housed.
Build all homes but add raised planters, sealed gardens and ongoing monitoring, reducing but not removing exposure risks.

title: Mine Dust and the Mothers' Petition
scenario: Union representative Alicia Condori at a copper mine in Peru is approached by mothers from a nearby community who say their children have respiratory problems linked to dust from the mine's open haul roads. Alicia's members, miners and their families, rely on the mine and fear that a campaign could prompt cutbacks. Management has offered a modest wetting programme. She can support the mothers' petition for an independent health study, quietly negotiate with management, or stay out.
options: Publicly back the petition for an independent health study, standing with the community even if the mine reacts.
Negotiate quietly with management for stronger dust controls, avoiding a public fight that could threaten jobs.
Remain neutral, concentrating on members' immediate interests and leaving the community to pursue its own route.
tension: solidarity with community vs. members' jobs

title: A Highway Through the Old Quarter
scenario: Transport planner Hyun-woo Baek in Seoul must choose between two routes for an expressway extension that would cut commutes for 90,000 daily drivers. One route passes through a wealthy hillside district with strong legal resources, adding nine minutes and 20 percent to the cost. The other cuts through an old working-class quarter with a large elderly population, where noise and pollution would rise. The ministry wants a recommendation within a month.
options: Recommend the cheaper, shorter route through the old quarter, maximising benefits to commuters and saving public funds.
Recommend the route through the wealthy district, accepting higher costs and legal fights to avoid burdening vulnerable residents.
Recommend the old-quarter route with a tunnel section and compensation package, raising costs but easing the impact.
tension: aggregate benefit vs. burden on vulnerable residents

title: Lead Pipes and the Rent Freeze
scenario: Municipal housing officer Gloria Mendoza in Manila learns that an old public tenement block has lead plumbing. Replacing the pipes requires emptying the building for several months, temporarily displacing 400 families into poorer, more distant housing. Leaving the pipes while installing point-of-use filters would be cheaper and avoid displacement but depends on residents maintaining filters properly. The risk from lead falls hardest on children and pregnant women. The budget decision is hers.
options: Replace the pipes and relocate residents temporarily, eliminating the hazard at a cost of disruption and hardship.
Install filters and a maintenance programme, keeping families in place and accepting residual risk.
Replace the pipes floor by floor with residents moving between units, a slower plan that prolongs exposure for some.

title: Cooling Pond or Fishing Village
scenario: Power station engineer Dmitri Sokolov in Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia region faces a choice during an energy crisis. Running the thermal plant at full output heats the nearby river through its cooling discharge beyond environmental permit limits, killing fish that a riverside community depends on. Reducing output would cause outages for homes and a hospital in winter. A regulator is aware of the limit but has not instructed him. Time is short.
options: Run at full output, keeping homes and the hospital powered and accepting the violation and fish kill.
Reduce output to stay within limits, protecting the river and the fishing community but causing outages.
Run at full output for hospital hours and reduce at night, a rotating arrangement that partly satisfies each need.

title: Rice Farmers Downstream of a Gold Mine
scenario: Journalist-turned-community-mediator Hasan Wibowo in Sulawesi, Indonesia, is asked by rice farmers to broker a deal with a gold mine whose mercury-laden runoff has damaged paddies. The mine offers compensation, a clean water system and local hiring, but demands that farmers sign away future claims. Some families need the money now, while others fear it will be worthless if the harm continues. Hasan must advise the farmers' assembly.
options: Advise signing the settlement, securing compensation and clean water immediately for struggling families.
Advise refusing to sign away future claims and pressing for independent monitoring first, accepting a longer wait.
Advise signing only a short-term interim agreement with review clauses, an arrangement the mine may reject.

title: The Petrochemical Plant in Cancer Alley
scenario: Parish council member Denise Thibodeaux in Louisiana must vote on a permit for a new plastics plant on land adjacent to a historically Black community already surrounded by chemical facilities. The company promises 300 jobs and tax revenue for the underfunded parish schools. Residents cite cancer clusters and want a moratorium on new permits. The vote is close, and she has been lobbied heavily from both sides.
options: Vote to approve with the strongest possible emission conditions, securing jobs and school funding.
Vote against and support a moratorium on additional permits, protecting a community that already carries heavy burdens.
Vote to table the permit pending an independent cumulative health assessment, delaying benefits and risking the company's withdrawal.
tension: jobs and school funding vs. cumulative health burden

title: E-Waste Yard and the Scrap Boys
scenario: NGO field officer Abena Owusu in Accra works near a scrapyard where teenagers burn cables to recover copper, exposing themselves and the neighbourhood to toxic smoke. The income helps pay school fees for siblings. A donor-funded clean recycling facility would offer safer work but pay less and employ only some of them. Authorities want to ban burning, though enforcement would likely drive it further out of sight. Abena must advise on how to proceed.
options: Push the authorities for a strict burning ban alongside the facility, prioritising health even if some teens lose income.
Work only with the facility and workers voluntarily, avoiding a ban that might push the burning underground.
Delay any ban until the facility can employ everyone currently working in the yard, leaving the smoke in place.
tension: health of youth and neighbourhood vs. income

title: Salt Flats and the Solar Farm
scenario: Regional planner Karla Mendes in Brazil's Rio Grande do Norte coast is reviewing plans for a large solar farm on land used by artisanal salt harvesters. The farm would supply power for 150,000 homes and bring investment, but the harvesters, families who have worked the pans for generations, would lose their livelihoods and have no formal title to the land. The company offers retraining, though the harvesters want a share of ownership.
options: Approve the project with the company's retraining offer, advancing clean energy and investment.
Deny approval until harvesters are granted title and a share of ownership, protecting their claim at the cost of delay.
Approve a smaller footprint that leaves part of the salt pans, reducing the clean energy yield and the harvesters' loss.

title: Noise, Dust and the Night Quarry
scenario: Quarry owner Stelian Dumitru in Romania has a contract to supply stone for a motorway and a rushed deadline, with penalties for lateness. Running the crushers through the night would meet the deadline but disturb a village of 900 residents with noise and dust, including a care home for the elderly. Daytime-only operation would risk the penalties and might cost the jobs of fifty workers. Municipal rules are ambiguous about night work.
options: Run the crushers at night, meeting the deadline and protecting jobs and the firm.
Operate during daytime only, respecting residents' rest and health and accepting penalties and possible job losses.
Run limited night shifts with dust suppression and a payment to the care home, a partial measure that may still cause distress.
tension: jobs and contract obligations vs. residents' wellbeing

title: Flood Relief for Whom First
scenario: Emergency coordinator Chanda Mulenga in Zambia has a limited number of water purification kits following floods that contaminated wells. The riverside informal settlement was hit hardest, while a nearby middle-class suburb has more registered residents, vocal officials and ready access to bottled water. Reports of cholera are coming from the settlement. The suburb's leaders insist on equal treatment and have called the minister. Chanda must split the kits.
options: Send nearly all kits to the settlement, where need and disease risk are highest.
Split the kits in proportion to population, treating the two areas equally on paper.
Send most kits to the settlement but a token share to the suburb, meeting need while managing political pressure.

title: Cement Works and the Asthma Ward
scenario: Paediatrician Dr. Rukhsana Qureshi in Karachi has recorded a rise in asthma cases among children living near a cement factory that supplies the construction of a new public hospital. She can publish her findings, which may lead to a shutdown or delay of the hospital project, or share them quietly with the factory owner in the hope of voluntary reductions. Her professional body is divided on the question.
options: Publish the findings, prioritising transparency and children's health despite the hospital's delay.
Share the findings privately with the owner and give him time to reduce emissions, risking continued exposure.
Share the findings with the regulator under confidentiality, hoping for a negotiated solution that leaves the project mostly intact.

title: Recycled Tyre Playground
scenario: Parks manager Nikolai Frolov in Estonia is considering building a playground surface from recycled tyre crumb, which is cheap, durable, and keeps tyres out of landfill. Some studies suggest trace chemicals could leach out, though results are mixed and no ban exists. Safer rubber alternatives cost twice as much and would mean building only one of the two planned playgrounds, one of which would serve a neglected housing estate.
options: Use the tyre crumb and build both playgrounds, giving more children access with an uncertain minor risk.
Use the safer alternative and build only one playground, avoiding potential risk while reducing access for others.
Use tyre crumb at the housing estate and the safer surface at the other, a split that could be seen as unfair.

title: Dumping Grounds and the Cousin's Contract
scenario: Contractor Siphiwe Zulu in KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa, has won a municipal contract to dispose of construction waste. The approved landfill is an hour away, and costs would cut his margin. His cousin, a farmer, offers a disused quarry near a poor settlement as a cheap unofficial dump, and the settlement's leaders would accept a small fee for access. Siphiwe's workers' wages depend on the contract holding. No one is likely to inspect the quarry.
options: Use the approved landfill, bearing the extra costs and thinner margin to avoid harming the settlement.
Use the quarry with the leaders' agreement, saving money and providing a small benefit to the settlement.
Use the approved landfill for hazardous materials and the quarry for clean rubble only, which reduces the harm and cost partially.
tension: legal compliance vs. profit and wages
consent of a poor community vs. environmental harm

title: Heat Island Trees on Rented Streets
scenario: Urban forester Chiara Esposito in Naples has funding to plant 2,000 street trees. Studies show the hottest, most treeless areas are poor neighbourhoods with narrow pavements and many renters, but planting there is harder, costs more and risks trees being vandalised or removed. Wealthier areas would have a higher survival rate and quick results, and residents there are asking loudly. The planting season is only a few weeks long.
options: Plant where trees are most likely to survive, maximising the number of healthy trees and total cooling.
Plant first in the hottest, poorest areas despite higher costs and lower survival, prioritising those who need shade most.
Plant half in each type of area, with community stewardship programmes for the poorer one, reducing the scale of both.

title: Asbestos Roofs and the Charity Hall
scenario: Volunteer coordinator Wanjiku Kariuki in Nairobi runs a community hall used as a school, clinic and meeting space in an informal settlement. The roof contains damaged asbestos sheets, and a visiting engineer says that removal by certified professionals costs more than the hall's annual funds. Local labourers offer to remove it cheaply but without protective equipment. Closing the hall would end services to hundreds of people. She has to decide this month.
options: Close the hall until professional removal can be funded, protecting people from asbestos but cutting services.
Allow the cheap removal by local labourers, keeping the hall open and accepting risks to the workers.
Keep the hall open with a temporary sealing of damaged areas while fundraising, which reduces but does not eliminate exposure.
tension: services now vs. long-term health risk

title: Fireworks Ban in the Valley
scenario: Mayor Hemant Joshi of a hill town in Uttarakhand, India, is under pressure to ban fireworks at the major annual festival after air monitors recorded dangerously high particulate levels, especially hazardous for the elderly and asthmatic children. Fireworks makers, many of them small family businesses, depend on this season for most of their yearly income, and the festival holds deep religious importance. A ban would likely lead to protests and some illicit sales.
options: Impose a full ban for the festival, protecting health at the expense of tradition and the makers' income.
Limit fireworks to certain hours and low-emission types, balancing health, tradition and livelihoods imperfectly.
Allow the festival as usual this year, issue health advisories and start consultations on a ban next year.

title: A Fish Farm Upstream of the Reindeer Lake
scenario: Aquaculture licensing officer Kirsten Aalto in northern Finland reviews an application for a salmon farm that would bring 40 jobs to a depopulating municipality. Effluent would add nutrients to a lake system downstream where Sami fishers and reindeer herders depend on clean water and fish. The company's modelling says the impact is minimal, but local knowledge holders disagree. Without the farm, the municipality's school may close.
options: Grant the licence with conditions and monitoring, supporting the municipality's survival and jobs.
Refuse the licence, protecting the downstream lake and Sami livelihoods despite the municipality's decline.
Defer the decision for a year to commission independent modelling with Sami participation, risking the company's departure.
tension: disputed evidence vs. need for action

title: Burning Rubbish Instead of Paying for Trucks
scenario: Village chief Hamidou Traoré in Mali manages a small settlement near a growing town where municipal rubbish collection has stopped for lack of funds. Residents are burning plastic waste, filling the village with smoke, while dumping it in the nearby wetland would risk water contamination. A private collector offers a service for a monthly fee that many families cannot afford. Hamidou has to decide how to organise waste for 1,200 people.
options: Contract the private collector and levy a flat household fee, ensuring regular service but burdening poorer families.
Organise a community dump on a hill away from the wetland, which is cheap and manageable but leaves environmental risks.
Ask the town authority to resume service under a collective petition, enduring smoke and mess until it responds.

title: Pesticide Drift Over the Schoolyard
scenario: Rural school principal Eduardo Villanueva in Argentina's Entre Rios province has seen crop-dusting planes spray fields beside his schoolyard during class hours, and some pupils have developed rashes and headaches. The farmers are his neighbours and employers of many parents, and aerial spraying is legal at the current distance. Reporting the problem could cost the school local goodwill and donations. He must decide whether to file a complaint.
options: File a formal complaint with the authorities, prioritising the pupils' health over relations with neighbours.
Speak privately with the farmers and ask for adjusted timing, preserving relations but relying on goodwill.
Do nothing formal but move outdoor activities and keep windows shut, avoiding conflict while leaving the practice unchanged.

title: Choosing the Dump Site After the Cyclone
scenario: Relief director Mere Vakatawa in Fiji must decide where to dispose of mountains of cyclone debris, including roofing, plastics and broken appliances. The cheapest site is a coastal mangrove flat beside a village that has been repeatedly passed over for aid. The alternative is a quarry in a wealthier district, requiring expensive trucking that would slow the clean-up of other storm-hit areas. Heavy rains are coming in two weeks.
options: Use the mangrove flat for rapid disposal, speeding the clean-up for the whole island.
Use the distant quarry, accepting delays elsewhere to avoid burdening a neglected village and its mangroves.
Use the mangrove flat only for inert debris and truck the rest to the quarry, taking some of both burdens.
tension: speed of recovery vs. fairness to a marginalised village
